subject: Post-demo: SLA tradeoffs for token bursts and streaming QoS
messages:
From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@signalshop.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 21 Jun 2027 10:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: SLA tradeoffs for token bursts and streaming QoS

Thanks again for the time today — great conversation and a good read on the SignalShop workload. I promised a short recap + clarifying asks so we can size a conservative staging replay and a recommended Dedicated starting config. See the attached throughput_profile.csv for the numbers I pulled from the demo traffic sample.

High-level takeaways from our call:
- Steady-state control plane: ~4–6 QPS for inference (non-embed endpoints) during off-peak.
- Peak bursts: short spikes to ~55–75 QPS for windows lasting ~60–120s, typically 2–3x per hour in the 09:00–11:00 local window.
- Average tokens per request: ~350–450 tokens (median ~390).
- Streaming required for the "guided response" endpoint (clients want partial results); first-byte latency target is ~400ms P95, end-to-end generation latency target ~1.5s P95 for typical requests.
- Concurrency: clients will open persistent streams from 10–30 concurrent sessions for high-traffic accounts; total concurrent in-flight requests can reach 120 during peaks.

Asks / clarifying items for your team (if you can reply inline):
1) Can you confirm the hourly pattern for weekday peaks (09:00–11:00 PST) is representative of production and not just the demo dataset?
2) For the guided-response streaming endpoint: is it acceptable to receive the first partial chunk within 400ms and then the rest streamed at ~200 tokens/sec?
3) Can you share 24–72 hours of anonymized request logs (top endpoints + timestamps + token counts) or a small sample export (sample_logs.zip) — that would let us run an accurate replay and surface tail latencies.

Proposed immediate plan:
- You provide sample logs by EOD Thu 6/24.
- Redwood runs a 72-hour replay on staging with current model + default quantization; we’ll report P50/P95/P99 latencies and recommended GPU counts.
- Deliver a short canary plan (how to rollout Dedicated nodes and autoscale thresholds) and a cost estimate within 5 business days of receiving logs.

Attachments: throughput_profile.csv (summary CSV)

Thanks — I’ll coordinate timing with Marissa and Karthik for the replay and canary notes.

—
Neha Kapoor

From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@signalshop.com>

Cc: Elena Morales <elena@signalshop.com>
Date: Mon, 21 Jun 2027 13:45:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Post-demo: SLA tradeoffs for token bursts and streaming QoS

Neha — thanks for the concise recap. A few quick clarifications from our side:

- The 09:00–11:00 window is correct for our East/US customers; we also see a smaller afternoon bump around 15:00–16:00. The demo sample was captured during a weekday peak, so it aligns.
- For streaming: first partial chunk within 400ms is ideal. The client-side expectation is that after the first partial chunk clients can accept a steady flow of ~150–250 tokens/sec; 200 tokens/sec is a good target.
- Concurrency: 120 concurrent in-flight is the upper bound; typical busy-minute concurrency is ~70–90.
- Endpoints: main inference endpoints are /v1/generate (75% of calls), /v1/stream (15%), and /v1/embed (10%). Embeddings are batched asynchronously and are less latency-sensitive.

I attached a small sample export (sample_logs.zip) — it's anonymized but includes timestamp, endpoint, request tokens, and a minimal request_id for correlation.

One more ask: can Redwood separately report first-byte vs full-response latencies in the staging replay? That split is important for our UX team to decide on client-side timeouts.

Happy to hop on a quick follow-up if that helps.

—
Alex Johnson
Head of Platform
SignalShop

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Post-demo: SLA tradeoffs for token bursts and streaming QoS

Looping in a quick technical read and initial sizing heuristics based on Alex's confirmations (copied below).

> Alex Johnson wrote:
> The 09:00–11:00 window is correct ... concurrency typical busy-minute ~70–90. Endpoints: /v1/generate 75%, /v1/stream 15%, /v1/embed 10%.

Sizing notes (initial conservative recommendation):
- Workload profile:
  - Steady QPS: plan for 6 QPS non-peak.
  - Peak burst: plan sustained 70 QPS for a 2-minute window as a conservative baseline (covers observed 55–75 range).
  - Avg tokens/request: 400 => token-rate during peak = 70 QPS * 400 tokens = 28k tokens/sec.
- Streaming: to meet first-byte P95 < 400ms and maintain 200 tokens/sec streaming, we need a setup that favors low per-request latency (single-request batching disabled for streaming path).

Redwood quick config suggestion (initial Dedicated baseline):
- 4 x A100-ish GPUs (or equivalent vGPUs) for steady state with autoscale policy to +4 GPUs on sustained CPU/GPU utilization or queueing for >30s.
- Prefix/KV cache enabled per customer to reduce repeated context costs (helps when bursts are driven by repeated prompt templates).
- Quantization: INT8/FP16 trial on non-stream endpoints to reduce per-token compute; keep streaming paths FP16 if you need deterministic latency.

Testing plan we can run once we have sample_logs.zip:
1) 72-hour replay on staging using your token distribution and real concurrency shape; measure: first-byte, streaming throughput, P50/P95/P99.
2) Run a second pass with quantized model to capture delta in latency and cost.
3) Produce canary rollout plan: start with 25% traffic on Dedicated nodes, ramp to 100% over 6–12 hours if SLOs hold.

Observability / deliverables:
- CSV of per-endpoint tail latencies, token cost estimate per 1M tokens, and recommended autoscale thresholds.
- Canary runbook with explicit fallback to hosted variant if errors or P95 > 2x target.

I can draft the canary runbook and cost spreadsheet once we have the logs. Recommend we also ask SignalShop if there are any scheduled marketing events next 30 days that might produce atypical surges.

—
Marissa Cole
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
